lecture.title: Abdominal Wall Hernias: Principles, Inguinal, Femoral, Ventral Hernias and Abdominal Wall Conditions
golden_tip: A tense, tender, irreducible hernia with no expansile cough impulse is strangulated until proven otherwise: gangrene may occur within 5-6 hours of the first symptom, so send for urgent surgery.

Normal or frequent bowel motions do NOT exclude strangulation when only part of the bowel circumference is trapped (Richter's hernia, usually femoral): constipation is late and perforation may occur before operation.

A pink serosanguineous discharge from a laparotomy wound around the 6th to 8th postoperative day is pathognomonic of burst abdomen; pain and shock are often absent, so never dismiss it as simple wound infection.
Neck above and medial to the pubic tubercle = inguinal hernia; below and lateral = femoral hernia. About half of femoral hernias present as emergencies, so every femoral hernia needs surgical repair.

A scar regains only 70% of initial muscle strength: 10% of laparotomy incisions and 1% of port sites herniate; close fascia with bites 5 mm apart and 5-8 mm from the edge at a 4:1 suture-to-wound ratio with 2/0 slowly resorbable suture.

concepts.title: Hernia Principles: Definition, Causes, Components and Classification
concepts.summary_ar: الفتق هو بروز غير طبيعي لعضو أو نسيج عبر فتحة في الطبقة التي تحصره عادة. يعتمد هذا المفهوم أسباب فتوق جدار البطن، والمكونات الأربعة للفتق (العيب والكيس والغلاف والمحتوى مع فتقي ريختر ولتري)، والتصنيف من الخفي إلى القابل للرد فغير القابل للرد فالمنسد فالمخنوق فالملتهب، مع التاريخ المرضي والفحص والتحري ومبادئ العلاج بما فيها المراقبة اليقظة والترقيع بالشبكة.

sections.heading: Definition and Learning Objectives
sections.body_text: A **hernia** is an abnormal protrusion of an organ or tissue through an opening in the layer that normally confines it. In the abdomen, viscera and peritoneal fat are pushed through a defect in the musculofascial wall and present as a lump, most often in the groin or around previous scars. This lecture sets eight learning objectives: (1) basic anatomy of the abdominal wall and its weaknesses; (2) causes of abdominal hernia; (3) types of hernia and classifications; (4) clinical history and examination findings in hernia; (5) complications of abdominal hernia; (6) non-surgical and surgical management of hernia including mesh; (7) complications of hernia surgery; and (8) other abdominal wall conditions. Mastering these objectives allows the student to manage one of the most common problems in general surgery, from a painless reducible groin lump to the life-threatening emergency of a strangulated hernia.
key_points: Hernia = abnormal protrusion of an organ or tissue through an opening in the layer that normally confines it.
Objectives: anatomy and weaknesses, causes, types and classification, clinical assessment, complications, management including mesh, complications of surgery, other abdominal wall conditions.

sections.heading: Causes of Abdominal Wall Herniation
sections.body_text:
Herniation requires a weak wall plus a driving force. The causes of abdominal wall herniation are:
- **Anatomical weakness** caused by inadequate muscular strength, classically at the **lumbar triangles** and the **posterior wall of the inguinal canal**.
- **Developmental failure of the processus vaginalis to close**, producing an **indirect inguinal hernia**.
- **Sharp and blunt trauma**: weakness may be the result of sharp trauma from abdominal surgery or stabbing. A surgical scar, even with perfect wound healing, has only **70% of the initial muscle strength**; consequently **10% of surgical incisions** and only **1% of laparoscopic port-site incisions** go on to herniate.
- **Genetic weakness of collagen**, aggravated by **smoking**.
- **Ageing and pregnancy**: herniation is common in pregnancy due to hormonally induced laxity of pelvic ligaments, and is more common in the elderly due to degenerative weakness of muscles and fibrous tissue.
- **Primary neurological and muscle diseases**.
- **Excessive intra-abdominal pressure** from chronic cough, straining on micturition or straining on defecation.
key_points: A surgical scar, even with perfect healing, retains only 70% of initial muscle strength.
10% of surgical incisions versus 1% of laparoscopic port-site incisions herniate.
Pressure factors: chronic cough, straining on micturition or on defecation.
Pregnancy causes hormonally induced laxity of pelvic ligaments; the elderly have degenerative weakness.

sections.heading: The Four Essential Components of an Abdominal Wall Hernia
sections.body_text:
Common principles in abdominal hernia: an abdominal wall hernia has four essential components.
- **1. A defect in the wall.** The weakness may be entirely in **muscle** (for example an incisional hernia), in **fascia** (for example an epigastric hernia through the linea alba), or it may have a **bony component** (for example a femoral hernia). The weakness in the wall is usually the **narrowest part of the hernia**. The defect varies in size and may be very small or indeed very large; a **small defect with rigid walls traps the content** and prevents it from freely moving in and out of the defect, increasing the risk of complications.
- **2. The sac of peritoneum.** More commonly, when peritoneum is lying immediately deep to the abdominal wall weakness, pressure forces the peritoneum through the defect and into the subcutaneous tissues. This sac of peritoneum allows bowel and omentum to pass through the defect.
- **3. The covering**, derived from the layers of the abdominal wall through which the sac passes.
- **4. The content**: omentum (**omentocele**); intestine (**enterocele** - small intestine, large intestine or appendix); a portion of the circumference of the intestine (**Richter's hernia**); a portion of bladder, ovary with or without fallopian tube; a **Meckel's diverticulum (Littre's hernia)**; or fluid as part of ascites.
key_points: Defect: in muscle (incisional), fascia (epigastric) or with a bony component (femoral).
The wall defect is usually the narrowest part of the hernia; small rigid defects trap content and cause complications.
Omentum = omentocele; intestine = enterocele; part of the bowel circumference = Richter's; Meckel's diverticulum = Littre's.
Other contents: portion of bladder, ovary with or without fallopian tube, fluid (ascites).

check.prompt: A hernia sac that contains a Meckel's diverticulum is called:
options: Littre's hernia
Richter's hernia
Omentocele
Bubonocele
Enterocele

sections.heading: Classification of Hernias Irrespective of Site
sections.body_text:
Classification (irrespective of the site):
- **1. Occult hernia** - not detectable clinically.
- **2. Reducible hernia** - the intraperitoneal organs can move freely in and out of the hernia; the content can be returned to the abdomen spontaneously, by the patient, or by the surgeon. There is an **expansile impulse on coughing**. If the content is **intestine**, there is a **gurgle on reduction and the first part is more difficult to reduce than the last**; if the content is **omentum**, it feels **doughy and the last portion is more difficult to reduce than the first**.
- **3. Irreducible hernia** - the content is unable to return to the peritoneal cavity due to adhesion, a small defect, or overcrowding within the sac; irreducibility of an omental hernia is diagnostic of an **omentocele**.
- **4. Obstructed hernia** - an irreducible hernia containing intestine which is partially or totally obstructed, but with **no interference with the blood supply** to the bowel. The symptoms are less severe and the onset more gradual than in strangulation.
- **5. Strangulated hernia** - the blood supply to the content is seriously impaired, making the contents ischemic. **Gangrene may occur 5-6 hours after the onset.** The wall of the bowel perforates, releasing infected, toxic bowel content into the tissues and ultimately back into the peritoneal cavity. Strangulation is **more common in femoral hernia** because of the **narrow neck and rigid surrounds**, and in **Richter's hernia**. On examination the hernia is **tense, tender, irreducible, with no expansile cough impulse**.
- **6. Inflamed hernia** - either from an internal cause, inflammation of the content of the sac (for example acute appendicitis or salpingitis), or from an external cause, a **trophic ulcer** that develops in the dependent part of a large hernia. On examination the hernia is **tender but not tense, with red, edematous overlying skin**.
key_points: Reducible intestine gurgles: first part hardest to reduce; omentum feels doughy: last portion hardest.
Obstructed = obstruction WITHOUT blood supply interference; strangulated = impaired blood supply, gangrene possible within 5-6 hours.
Strangulated hernia O/E: tense, tender, irreducible, no expansile cough impulse.
Strangulation is commonest in femoral hernia (narrow neck, rigid surroundings) and Richter's hernia.
Inflamed hernia: tender, NOT tense, red edematous skin (internal cause like appendicitis/salpingitis, or trophic ulcer).

check.prompt: What distinguishes an obstructed hernia from a strangulated hernia?
options: The blood supply to the bowel is intact in obstruction but impaired in strangulation
Obstruction is always painless whereas strangulation is always painless too
Strangulation has a longer and more gradual onset
Obstruction occurs only in femoral hernias
Strangulated hernias always contain omentum
check.explanation_ar: الفتق المنسد يحتوي أمعاء مسدودة جزئياً أو كلياً مع بقاء التروية الدموية سليمة وأعراضه أخف وبدايته أكثر تدرجاً، بعكس الفتق المخنوق الذي تختل فيه التروية الدموية فيصبح المحتوى ناقص التروية وعرضة للغنغرينا خلال 5-6 ساعات.

sections.heading: Clinical History, Examination and Investigations
sections.body_text:
**History.** Self-diagnosis is common. The hernia is usually painless, but patients may complain of an aching or heavy feeling. Sharp, intermittent pain suggests pinching of tissue, and **severe pain should alert the surgeon to a high risk of strangulation**. One should determine whether the hernia reduces spontaneously or needs to be helped. The patient should be asked about symptoms which might suggest bowel obstruction. It is important to know if this is a primary hernia, a recurrent hernia or an incisional hernia after previous surgery. General questions regarding the cardiac and respiratory systems are necessary to assess anaesthetic risk. In a male with a groin hernia, take a history of prostatic symptoms.
**Examination checks.** Reducibility; cough impulse; overlying skin color changes (**bruising suggests venous engorgement of the content, while overlying cellulitis means the hernia content is strangulating**); tenderness; multiple defects and the contralateral side; signs of previous repair; scrotal content for a groin hernia; associated pathology.
**Investigations.** For most hernias, no specific investigation is required, the diagnosis being made on clinical examination. Plain x-ray is of little value. Ultrasound scan is low cost but operator dependent, and may be useful in the early postoperative period. CT scan is used in complex ventral and incisional hernia. MRI scan is good in sportsman's groin with pain from an orthopaedic injury. Laparoscopy is useful to identify an occult contralateral inguinal hernia.
key_points: Severe pain in a hernia = high risk of strangulation.
Bruising over a hernia suggests venous engorgement; cellulitis suggests strangulating content.
Always examine for multiple defects, the contralateral side, signs of previous repair and scrotal content.
US: cheap, operator dependent, useful early postoperatively; CT: complex ventral/incisional; MRI: sportsman's groin; laparoscopy: occult contralateral hernia.

sections.heading: Principles of Management: Watchful Waiting, Truss and Repair
sections.body_text:
An abdominal wall hernia does not necessarily require repair. **Surgery** is indicated for relief of symptoms of discomfort and for cosmesis, when complications are likely, in **all cases of femoral hernia** because of the high risk of strangulation, in **any case of irreducible hernia**, especially where there is pain and tenderness, and it should be offered to younger adult patients. A patient who presents with **acute pain in a hernia, particularly if it is irreducible, should be offered urgent surgery**.
In elderly patients a policy of **watchful waiting** in asymptomatic inguinal hernia appears generally safe, provided the hernia is asymptomatic, small in size, easily reduced and is not causing anxiety. A **truss** can be used to control a hernia.
Large incisional hernias, particularly recurrent ones, present a major problem: surgical repair is a complex procedure with significant risk of complications and later recurrence. When the neck is wide, the risk of strangulation is low; in the obese and elderly patient these risks may outweigh the benefits of surgery, so surgeons commonly adopt a conservative approach.
**Modern surgical repairs follow four principles:** (1) reduction of the hernia contents into the abdominal cavity with excision of any non-viable tissue and bowel repair if necessary; (2) excision and closure of the peritoneal sac; (3) closure of the hernia defect if possible; (4) reinforcement of the abdominal wall with **mesh**.
key_points: All femoral hernias and all irreducible hernias (especially painful ones) need surgery; acute painful irreducible hernia = urgent surgery.
Watchful waiting is safe in elderly patients with asymptomatic, small, easily reduced, non-anxiety-causing inguinal hernia.
Wide-necked large incisional hernias in the obese/elderly may be treated conservatively.
Repair principles: reduce contents + excise non-viable tissue, excise and close the sac, close the defect, reinforce with mesh.

check.prompt: Which hernia must always be offered surgical repair because of its high risk of strangulation?
options: Femoral hernia
Asymptomatic small epigastric hernia containing fat only
Divarication of the recti abdominis
Small asymptomatic paraumbilical hernia without bowel
Any occult hernia detected on laparoscopy

فتق الثرب: فتق محتواه كتلة من الثرب (الأومنتوم).

concepts.title: Inguinal Hernia: Surgical Anatomy, Embryology and Types
concepts.summary_ar: يشرح هذا المفهوم التشريح الجراحي للقناة الإربية (الحلقة العميقة والحلقة السطحية والحدود والأعصاب الثلاثة) ونشأة الفتق غير المباشر من بقاء الناتئ المهبلي مفتوحاً، ثم أنواع الفتق الإربي: غير المباشر بأنواعه الثلاثة (البوبونوسيل والحبلي والكامل)، والمباشر عبر مثلث هسلباخ، والمنزلق بمحتوياته المميزة حسب الجهة.

sections.heading: Overview and Surgical Anatomy of the Inguinal Canal
sections.body_text:
Inguinal hernia is the most common hernia in men and is around **10 times more common in men than in women**. There are two basic types, indirect and direct, plus a third pattern, the sliding hernia.
**Surgical anatomy.** The **deep inguinal ring** is a defect in the transversalis fascia lying midway between the pubic tubercle and the anterior superior iliac spine, about **2-3 cm above and marginally lateral to the femoral artery pulse** in the groin. The **inferior epigastric vessels** lie just medial to the deep inguinal ring, passing from the iliac vessels to the rectus abdominis muscle. The transversus muscle and the internal oblique muscle arch over the deep inguinal ring to become attached to the pubic tubercle, forming the **conjoint tendon**; below this arch there is no muscle, only transversalis fascia, resulting in an **area of weakness**. Anterior to the canal is the aponeurosis of the external oblique muscle, the fibers of which run downwards and medially; the testis finally emerges through an inverted V-shaped defect in this aponeurosis, the **superficial inguinal ring, 1.25 cm above the pubic tubercle**, and descends into the scrotum.
**Boundaries of the inguinal canal:** anterior = external oblique aponeurosis; posterior = transversalis fascia (with the inferior epigastric vessels medial to the deep ring); superior = conjoint tendon; inferior = inguinal ligament.
**The canal** is **3.75 cm long** in the adult, directed **downward and medially**. It transmits the **spermatic cord**: testicular artery, veins, lymphatics and the vas deferens. In females the **round ligament** descends through the canal to end in the labia majora. **Three important nerves** are related to the canal: the **ilioinguinal**, the **iliohypogastric** and the **genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve**.
key_points: Inguinal hernia is about 10 times more common in men than in women.
Deep ring: transversalis fascia defect midway between pubic tubercle and ASIS, 2-3 cm above and slightly lateral to the femoral artery pulse.
Superficial ring: inverted V-shaped defect in external oblique aponeurosis, 1.25 cm above the pubic tubercle.
Canal = 3.75 cm in adults, downward and medial; transmits spermatic cord (or round ligament to the labia majora).
Nerves: ilioinguinal, iliohypogastric, genital branch of genitofemoral.
Weakness below the arch of the conjoint tendon: only transversalis fascia, no muscle.

sections.heading: Embryology: Processus Vaginalis and Congenital Hernia
sections.body_text: As the testis descends, a tube of peritoneum is pulled with the testis and wraps around it, ultimately forming the **tunica vaginalis**. This peritoneal tube should obliterate, possibly under hormonal control, but it commonly fails to fuse either in part or totally. As a result, bowel within the peritoneal cavity is able to pass inside the tube down towards the scrotum. **Inguinal hernia in neonates and young children is always of this congenital type.** However, in other patients the muscles around the deep inguinal ring can prevent a hernia from developing until later in life, when, under the constant positive abdominal pressure, the deep inguinal ring and muscles are stretched and the hernia becomes apparent.
key_points: Patent processus vaginalis (partial or total) allows bowel to pass towards the scrotum.
Inguinal hernia in neonates and young children is ALWAYS congenital.
In adults, the deep ring and muscles stretch under constant positive abdominal pressure until the hernia appears.

sections.heading: Indirect (Oblique, Lateral) Inguinal Hernia
sections.body_text:
The indirect hernia is **lateral** because its origin is lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, and **oblique** because the hernia passes obliquely from lateral to medial through the abdominal muscle layers. It is the **most common type of hernia**, is common in the young, and affects **males 10 times more than females**. In the first decade it is more common on the **right** side. Clinical features include pain in the groin **referred to the testicles** when performing heavy work or taking strenuous exercise, visible and palpable bulging on coughing, and, as time goes on, the hernia comes down as soon as the patient stands up. In a large hernia there is a sensation of weight and dragging on the mesentery, producing **epigastric pain**. In an infant the swelling appears when the child cries.
**Types of indirect inguinal hernia:**
- **1. Bubonocele** - the hernia is limited to the inguinal canal.
- **2. Funicular** - the processus vaginalis is closed just above the epididymis, so the content of the sac is felt separately from the testis.
- **3. Complete (scrotal)** - common in infancy, and also in adolescence and adult life; the testis appears to lie within the lower part of the hernia.
key_points: Indirect = lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, oblique course, most common type, young males (M:F = 10:1).
Right side predominates in the first decade.
Bubonocele: confined to the canal; funicular: sac felt separately from the testis; complete (scrotal): testis lies within the lower part of the hernia.
Large indirect hernias cause dragging pain on the mesentery felt as epigastric pain.

check.prompt: An indirect hernia whose sac is felt separately from the testis because the processus vaginalis is closed just above the epididymis is a:
options: Funicular hernia
Bubonocele
Complete scrotal hernia
Direct hernia
Sliding hernia
